**Each person owns specific chores (B)** tends to work well when:
- People have clear preferences (someone doesn't mind dishes but hates bathrooms)
- You want accountability (it's obvious who dropped the ball)
- You value low overhead (no tracking who's up this week)

**A weekly rotation (A)** tends to work well when:
- Chores are unevenly unpleasant and you want to share the burden fairly
- You want everyone to stay capable of doing everything
- No one wants to be "stuck" with the worst job permanently

I gave B a slight edge because fixed ownership usually reduces friction and finger-pointing, but if your least-favorite chores are wildly worse than others, a rotation (or a hybrid where you rotate only the dreaded tasks) may be fairer.

**B**

Fixed ownership generally works better. When each person permanently owns specific chores, accountability is unambiguous — if the trash overflows, everyone knows whose job it was. People also get faster and more consistent at tasks they do repeatedly, and they can trade based on preference (someone who hates dishes but doesn't mind bathrooms can swap), which makes the whole arrangement feel less burdensome.

Rotations create a recurring coordination cost — someone has to track whose week it is — and they invite disputes about whether the last person actually finished. They also produce a "not my week, not my problem" attitude toward messes that appear off-schedule.

The main caveat: ownership only works if the chores are roughly equal in effort and unpleasantness. If one job is clearly the worst (cleaning the shared bathroom, say), rotating *that specific chore* while keeping the rest fixed is a reasonable hybrid.
